items.question: How do you think about using recent AI progress to predict when AI will fully automate remote work?
items.object: Extrapolating recent AI progress to forecast full automation of remote work
items.answer: So I think that a lot of people have this intuition that progress has been very fast. They look at the trend lines and just extrapolate; obviously, it's going to happen in, I don't know, 2027 or 2030 or whatever. They're just very bullish. And obviously, that's not a thing you can literally do. There isn't a trend you can literally extrapolate of “when do we get to full automation?” Because if you look at the fraction of the economy that is actually automated by AI, it's very small. So if you just extrapolate that trend, which is something, say, Robin Hanson likes to do, you're going to say, “Well, it's going to take centuries” or something. Now, we don't agree with that view. But I think one way of thinking about this is: how many big things are there? How many core capabilities, competencies are there that the AI systems need to be good at in order to have this very broad economic impact, maybe 10x acceleration and growth or something? How many things have you gotten over the past 10 years, 15 years?

The response proposes assessing prospects for broad AI-driven economic transformation by comparing the core capabilities still needed with those acquired over the past 10–15 years.

items.question: Why do you think being connected to a research community matters for doing mathematics research?
items.object: Access to a research community's information when doing mathematics research
items.answer: I think this is true even in academic fields. So if you want to do math research, but you're not part of a graduate program, you're not at a university where there are tons of people who do math research all day for many years, then you're not even going to know what are the open problems that I should be working on? What is reasonable to attack? What is not reasonable to attack? What papers in this field are important, contain important techniques? You're just going to have no idea. So it's very important to be plugged into that feed of information somehow.

items.question: How do you think someone outside an intellectual community can use the internet to find people worth learning from?
items.object: Finding interesting thinkers through the internet and intellectual social networks
items.answer: I think the internet is a pretty useful thing in this respect. You don't need to necessarily talk to people, you can get a lot of benefit from reading. But you just need to identify, who are the people who seem constantly most interesting? And maybe you find one person. And then often that person will know some other people who are interesting. And then you can start tracing the social network. One example I can give, which I think is actually accurate, is maybe you know about Daniel Ellsberg. So you look for a podcast he appears on. You notice that he's appeared on 80,000 Hours podcast, which he has. And then you notice there are some other guests on the 80,000 Hours podcast. So maybe there's Bryan Caplan, who has also appeared on the podcast. And then maybe Robin Hanson has also appeared on the podcast. And then maybe there are some people those other people know. And then just tracing that kind of social network and figuring out who to listen to like that. And I think you're doing a very big service to making that possible. I think your selection is often very good.

items.question: Why did you want GATE to model economic decisions through optimization?
items.answer:
Maybe the biggest one was that in that model, economic decisions were hardcoded. They were not made in the standard way that this would typically be done in the economics literature, which would be that you would have some kind of utility or value function, and then you would be optimizing that to get the best outcome, maybe under certain constraints. Instead of doing that, it was just a bunch of hardcoded rules, little parameters that I think the Open Phil folks just thought made sense. But that meant if you used relatively extreme parameter values or something, the decisions would look very unreasonable. So that was the main motivation to turn it into a standard economic model. This would also allow us to answer questions that the original model could not. You could say, okay, suppose that people assign such-and-such credence to AGI being capable of full automation, let's say 10%. They're not sure, maybe they're uncertain. Then what should they do? How much should they invest? There are these interesting possibilities where people might invest a bunch early if that helps them resolve the uncertainty. Maybe they observe the slope of the automation curve to see, okay, does this thing look like it's going to get full automation? Maybe it does, maybe it doesn't.

So they might update on that, and that might inform their investment decisions, which we can observe in GATE, which you couldn't observe in this older framework because all the decisions had been hardcoded. So that's the basic motivation. It's important to not oversell the model in the sense that it's not really meant to be a predictive model. It's meant to be more like, as I think Tom Davidson's original model was, not really meant to be predictive. In fact, a lot of economics models are not really meant to be predictive. They are more meant to show you what happens in this simulated world where certain mechanisms are built into the world and certain ones might be left out. But I think a lot of people's thinking about AI can be incoherent in the sense that they might believe things that are actually incompatible with each other, and this kind of model helps clarify that.

items.question: Why are you skeptical that automating AI research alone would remove the main constraints on AI progress?
items.object: Complementarity in AI research and development
items.answer: I'm not sure if you can actually automate the process of R&D without also automating much of the rest of the economy, at least the remote parts of the economy. Even if you do automate R&D, it's not clear how much that gets you if you can't automate the scaling of compute. If you think the scaling of compute has been the key driver of the rapid software progress over the past 10 to 15 years, then you wouldn't necessarily be resolving that bottleneck by just scaling the researcher population much faster. There's a question about to what extent research efforts from humans or possibly AIs, compute for useful experiments, and maybe to some extent real-world data, insofar as that matters, are complements. I would assume that these are complements, and if you just scale one of them by orders of magnitude while the other one remains flat, then you're just going to get bottlenecked and it's not going to have as big of an impact as you might have thought.

items.question: How do you distinguish R&D being essential for long-run economic growth from R&D accounting for most growth?
items.answer:
If you do growth accounting, what you find is that total factor productivity growth is only a fraction of long-run growth. The part of that driven by explicit R&D instead of things like learning by doing or economies of scale—you're just more efficient at producing things because you operate on a larger scale—or better management, better coordination, less misallocation of resources: all those things affect productivity. The part driven by explicit R&D is a fraction. Basically, the part of economic growth driven by R&D directly is a fraction of a fraction of all economic growth.

So it ends up being fairly small compared to what people think, which is that almost all of it is driven by R&D. That's not true. But I think people can misunderstand this claim and say, “Well, if you didn't have any R&D, we wouldn't have grown since the 1700s, and we wouldn't have our current level of wealth and prosperity.” That's true, but that just means R&D is essential for long-run growth. A lot of other things are also essential. Imagine that we had done R&D since 1700 but hadn't scaled our capital stock at all. We would again be very poor now. That doesn't mean that just because multiple things can be essential for long-run growth, labor isn't also essential. You get a direct benefit from increased output, and output is a big labor, but on top of that you get to use labor to drive R&D. You can use the workers as researchers, or use the big economy that the workers provide to make serendipitous discoveries. AI is just going to scale that a bunch as well.

That seems like a much more relevant channel than narrowly deploying the AIs to do R&D. If you have the choice, it's much more economically valuable to deploy the AI to do broad labor tasks. You would also do R&D, sure, but in the end all the factors of production would need to scale for you to get long-run growth. If you did growth accounting, you would see that most of it is coming from the scaling of labor and capital, and relatively little is coming from R&D. I wouldn't expect that trend to change particularly with AI.

items.question: How do you think AI labs’ financial incentives shape their willingness to deploy AI for basic research?
items.object: AI labs’ incentives to conduct scientific research
items.answer: There is a sense in which even the social value of R&D, which does exist and is essential for long-run growth, even if it's not literally the most important thing that drives it, is still a key bottleneck that we need to get past. Even that social value is mostly external, which means that if you're an AI lab, you don't get most of the value from doing the R&D. Software R&D is a bit different because you internalize the value at least to some extent. There are multiple competitors, so you don't totally internalize it, but to some extent. If you're doing biology R&D or basic research, you internalize almost none of the value. Even if that is very socially valuable, you would probably still not do it very much because you don't internalize the value. You would prioritize things that make you money. That would allow you to increase your valuation and raise more capital and make more money to reinvest more into AI and so on.

items.question: How do you assess the safety implications of AI development being shaped by broad economic and political forces?
items.object: Broad AI deployment and safety governance
items.answer:
In general, the broader the scale of the changes and deployment is going to be, the more you should expect that what happens is not driven by the idiosyncrasies or management decisions of any particular lab. It's more shaped by general economic, social, or political forces. There are a lot more abilities for those forces to operate and control what's happening, and I agree that's the most plausible outcome. If you're worried about AI, that's not necessarily reassuring, because you might think those forces themselves are going to make decisions that you don't like. It's a bit unclear if you're worried about the safety aspect of it whether that's actually better or worse. Maybe you're the kind of person who just believes in one lab, like Anthropic is great, and it's good if they win, and it's better if they have this lead. Then it's not actually that good if they have to submit to markets and political pressures and make their systems the way other people want them to be.

On the other hand, if you're not particularly impressed by the track record of AI safety inside the big labs, then you might see this as a welcome development. Maybe you think broader oversight and disciplining forces are going to be helpful. People care a lot about safety in other industries, especially when there's a visible disaster or safety failure. Safety can become a very large priority. Maybe that kind of thing might happen, in which case this might be good from your point of view.

items.question: How do you think AI automation will affect human wages over time?
items.answer:
Economically, it's a complex question. I think it's much easier to predict that eventually wages are going to fall below subsistence, at least for biological humans, than to predict when that will happen. As you scale up your capital and labor stock, you hit diminishing returns that lower the marginal value of those things, and wages are just the marginal product of labor. So you expect those to fall, but at the same time there's an opposing effect because you're going to be getting increased total factor productivity, and that could cancel the falling wages you would otherwise expect from the increase in labor, at least up to a certain point. Maybe eventually it doesn't work, but up to a certain point. The timescale is unclear. It also depends on how fast the world economy grows, because the faster we grow, the faster we reach the bottlenecks. If growth is very slow, this could take centuries; if it's very fast, as fast as we think, maybe it only takes decades.

But even after you reach full automation, it's not clear if they're below where they used to be because of this total factor productivity effect. Otherwise, I agree with that story. Initially, when you get 50%, 60%, 70% automation, the wages of the people who are still employed are going to be much higher in real terms. There's going to be a question about to what extent people can reallocate from the tasks that just got automated to the tasks that are not yet automated. If they can do that, you don't necessarily see a lot of unemployment early on. But maybe they can't do that very effectively; maybe it's not worth it. If the automation is proceeding very quickly and you need a year to acquire the skills that are going to make you effective at this new occupation, but that thing is going to be automated in a year anyway, then you might not even invest the effort. You might just, quote unquote, give up because it's not going to be worth it.

items.question: Why do you think learning a skill can remain valuable even when language models become better at it than you?
items.object: Human expertise as a complement to language models
items.answer:
I think there's an extent to which your skills are, to some extent, a complementary package. Just because models are better than you at X doesn't mean the skill X has become not valuable for humans. It might not be easy to find a person who has skills Y and Z and can use the AI to make up for their shortcoming in X, compared to a person who has all three skills and can do them as a package and benefit from synergies and complementarities. Someone having those skills just makes them more productive in other ways. I would maybe not be quite as pessimistic. I would still recommend that you probably have enough time for learning these things to pay off, but I think it would pay off in a somewhat different way than you might expect.

If you want to hire someone, it's much less convenient to hire a person who's good at some other skills but not good at math, and then tries to compensate for that weakness by using LMs to remedy that. Even if LMs become superhuman at math, that still doesn't mean that you don't want to hire people who are good at math, because there's a way in which the LM skill is more difficult to integrate into your normal workflow compared to a person who would just have the same skills, maybe not as good, but as part of a complementary package with a lot of other skills, many of which the LM can't do at all right now. Such a person will probably be more effective at operating the LLM and driving it towards the results they want. I think this is true right now, but if you don't know any math, it's hard to notice when the LM makes a mistake.

You basically can't evaluate the outputs of the model if you don't know what it's doing.

And it's just harder to drive it. For example, if you're using a language model for creative writing, you need to have good taste to say what is a good output, what is a bad output, and do I want to change this or keep this? Even though LLMs are already in some ways better at writing than most people, the people who are actually good at it can still leverage it and use it as a multiplier. They resample a bunch of times and recommend edits: “This doesn't look quite as good; can you redo this part?” It makes them more productive, not less productive.

items.question: How do you expect transformer-based AI systems to acquire new capabilities over the next five years?
items.object: Transformer architecture and changing training methods
items.answer: I don't really expect big changes in architecture in the next five years, because a transformer has been surprisingly long-lived. We should expect that to continue, but we have seen a lot of changes in how people train transformers. It's the same architecture, but used in very different ways. We first had pretraining on next-token prediction. Before that we had things like translation from English to French, the original application of the transformer. Then with BERT in 2018 from Google, the training objective was: we give you a sentence, mask some of the words, and then you predict them. Then it became less of a prediction, the GPT paradigm, and that has stuck. Then we started doing post-training: RLHF, now a different kind of RL with reasoning. We have synthetic data pipelines, and long-context fine-tuning, a new thing that's emerged maybe in the past three years. We've seen all these changes in how transformers are trained, so we should continue to expect that. The new capabilities that are unlocked are likely to be associated with a different way to train it on different data using a different kind of signal for RL, or maybe some totally different way of training it. I think the architecture will continue being stable just because that's likely to continue to be stable.

We have synthetic data pipelines, and long-context fine-tuning, a new thing that's emerged maybe in the past three years. We've seen all these changes in how transformers are trained, so we should continue to expect that. The new capabilities that are unlocked are likely to be associated with a different way to train it on different data using a different kind of signal for RL, or maybe some totally different way of training it. I think the architecture will continue being stable just because that's likely to continue to be stable.

rubrics.text: The response expects transformer architecture to remain broadly stable over the next five years.
The response expects new capabilities to emerge through changes in how transformers are trained.

items.question: What do you see as the promise and limitation of using human data to bootstrap reinforcement learning for difficult AI capabilities?
items.object: Human demonstrations as a starting point for reinforcement learning
items.answer:
I think the obvious thing is to try the thing that led to the original AlphaGo, which is to collect a lot of human data. I'm not sure what the human data would look like or what form it would have to take. It's a bit unclear. Then hope that fine-tuning on that gives you enough traction for some kind of reinforcement learning pipeline to have enough signal to get working. The problem with doing reinforcement learning naively is that the reward signals might be too sparse, so you might not get anywhere. You need the model to have a certain level of competence from the start for a very naive RL approach to work. That would be my first guess, and maybe it's still going to work. It's hard to say, because you could have said reinforcement learning was not going to work for complex reasoning because if it would have worked, someone would have done it already. But it turns out it works. Maybe you'll see something similar.

The main doubt I have is that the human data you collect might not be what you actually need. You might need data about what's going on in their brain and not what they're doing externally in their behavior. That's how it doesn't work to train a reasoning model whose fine-tuning is on arXiv papers, because that's not actually relevant data. Relevant data is probably something that's going on in the head. That would be pretty difficult to acquire. We don't know how to extract that knowledge.

items.question: Why do you think AI benchmarks tend to get saturated so quickly?
items.object: Selection effects in AI benchmark saturation
items.answer:
I think there's an answer to why benchmarks get saturated so quickly: people only build a benchmark when solving it appears to be in sight. We don't make a benchmark that's completely impossible, like, can GPT-4 cook me a meal?

That's not a benchmark. It doesn't exist because it would be pointless to get zeros for many years. But we can already imagine a benchmark about whether GPT-4 can do computer-use tasks reasonably well. OSWorld is kind of like that, except OSWorld tasks are very narrow and specific. You can imagine a more general benchmark about that, and the fact you can imagine that benchmark probably means that's going to happen. You're imagining it because it seems plausible to you that it might happen on some level.

Labs also pay for benchmarks when they think the payoff is going to be fairly soon. There's economic selection: the benchmarks that get lab funding are the benchmarks that labs expect to be useful in the near term, not just for demos and making their models seem impressive, but also for internal evals. If every single model always gets zero on a benchmark, you get no useful internal signal for decisions about what to do. You need some variation in model performance, which means the models already have to be somewhat competent on the benchmarks. I think that's a lot of what's going on. You wouldn't expect us to get to the dream benchmark where you see smooth performance over time. Maybe that would happen, but I think it would be by accident. It's hard to design that in advance.

items.question: Why do you think evolution is better understood as algorithm architecture search than as a training run for the human brain?
items.answer:
The point is that if doing a task was very valuable in the evolutionary environment and has been valuable for a very long time, then there's been a lot of selection pressure applied. The way those capabilities are instantiated or implemented in the human brain—the algorithms used to do those things—are very sophisticated. You don't get a lot of trained parameters or whatever from evolution, because DNA doesn't contain that much information. DNA only contains enough information to code for an algorithm and high-level details. You can't view evolution as analogous to a training run, with the results going into your brain, because there isn't that much information in the genome. But you can view it as analogous to algorithm architecture search.

The algorithms are very separate. The brain has different regions responsible for different things: the cerebellum has its own responsibilities, separate from the rest of the brain. It has specific areas devoted to visual processing, audio processing, general-purpose thinking in the prefrontal cortex, language understanding, and parsing. These are all very regional and probably done by different kinds of algorithms to some extent, because they're regional and the same areas are in everyone. It has to be coded in the genome somewhere that that's how it happens.

items.question: How do you expect AI’s management capabilities to become recognized in practice?
items.answer:
AI remains less data-efficient than humans, so we need more data if you want to teach something to an AI. But if humans are bad enough, maybe you don't even need that much data for the machine to do a better job than humans. The question is, how would you even find out if this is the case? Management is not something you can have a good benchmark for. You need to convince people to show up and work for you. It seems difficult to convince people that this is actually the case.

It's the kind of capability that might emerge, and people might only realize that AI has that capability significantly later. I think people will be trying to find ways to integrate AI into their workflow, and that's probably the channel through which it's going to happen. It's not going to happen by AI labs saying, “We're going to replace management.” It'll be more like managers themselves, especially ones more familiar with the technology, start using it more and notice that it benefits them. One very simple thing is that a manager has to read a lot of stuff. You can imagine a very competent AI speeding that up enormously: “What is this? Find this information in these documents; check this for that.” Those are very simple things, which are very simple to an AI but time-consuming to a human, that you can outsource to an AI. That could be one.

items.question: What do you think current long-context evaluations miss about language models’ practical limitations?
items.answer:
Currently the models' performance degrades quite a lot if you try to use them in any kind of longer context. It's not just about the context window limits you see, like, “We can only handle 200,000 tokens in one context.” That's fake. They can't handle 200,000 tokens without loss of performance. The benchmarks they have for testing long-context performance are very narrow. They're things like needle-in-a-haystack evaluations, where you just have to find some specific thing in a long passage of text. But what matters more is: if I give you a long document, how much do you hallucinate about it? How much do you understand if different parts of it are interacting with each other? If you talk with a language model over a long context—for example, have it write a story for you—you'll notice that even after you get past tens of thousands of tokens, low tens of thousands, its coherence and ability to understand what's going on, recall details, and make inferences based on what has been written in the past context starts getting worse. I don't know how this will be solved. Maybe it will be solved by fine-tuning on more long-context things.

I'm not sure what the key thing is going to be, but it seems like a big issue because long context is required for unlocking a lot of economically valuable applications. Even 200,000 tokens is not that long. That's not enough to fit a good chunk of Harry Potter books; you can fit a single book into a context. That makes it much more annoying to use. If these models had tens of millions of tokens of context and could do that without noticeable loss in performance, and maybe without a steep increase in price, which is what you might get today because of the complexity of attention, I think that would be valuable and unlock a lot of other economically valuable applications. Once you have a model that's really performant at long context, you might train it much better to use that long context for other things, like reasoning. That seems like a relevant bottleneck to me. Another possibility is that agency gets quite a bit better, but I'm not sure.
